papers.title: Reversal of refractory epilepsy in an adult with GAMT deficiency: A case report and comparative literature review.
papers.abstract: Guanidinoacetate methyltransferase (GAMT) deficiency is a rare autosomal recessive creatine biosynthesis disorder. Reports specifically focusing on adult patients remain scarce. We report a 52-year-old female (the oldest documented case of GAMT deficiency to date) presenting with severe intellectual disability, refractory epilepsy, and adult-onset disease progression. Whole-exome sequencing identified novel compound heterozygous GAMT variants (c.265_267del and c.253G>T), and magnetic resonance spectroscopy confirmed cerebral creatine depletion. Remarkably, initiating oral creatine supplementation at age 52 achieved complete seizure freedom, normalization of the electroencephalogram (EEG), and significant motor function recovery. A comprehensive review revealed that untreated adult patients face a high risk of progressive neurological deterioration. Compared to the pediatric cohort, adults exhibited a significantly higher prevalence of movement disorders (69.2% vs. 33.1%, p < 0.001) and a trend toward a higher prevalence of epilepsy (92.3% vs. 74.2%). Especially, atonic seizures (drop attacks) are particularly characteristic of adult GAMT deficiency, with EEGs frequently demonstrating background slowing, multifocal epileptiform discharges, and electrodecremental patterns. This study underscores that continuous disease progression and prolonged neurotoxicity still could compromise the well-being of adult GAMT deficiency patients. Accurate diagnosis is essential for adults presenting with developmental and epileptic encephalopathy (DEE) phenotype, as even late treatment for GAMT deficiency can still dramatically alleviate the epileptic burden and reverse motor decline. We report the oldest known adult diagnosed with GAMT deficiency. Our case demonstrates that starting creatine treatment even at age 52 can dramatically reduce seizures and restore motor function. Literature shows that untreated adults suffer from more severe epilepsy and movement disorders than children, with symptoms worsening over time. These findings highlight the critical need for genetic testing in adults with unexplained severe epilepsy; timely creatine supplementation can halt cognitive decline and significantly restore quality of life.

papers.title: Perceptions of Intra-Operative EEG Brain Monitoring During Pediatric Anesthesia Among Children and Parents: An Exploratory Cross-Sectional Survey.
papers.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) monitoring during pediatric anesthesia may improve perioperative safety by optimizing anesthetic titration and reducing adverse outcomes. However, little is known about patient and caregiver perceptions regarding this technology and its implementation into routine anesthesia care. This study evaluates perceived importance, utility, and extent of reassurance provided by intra-operative EEG monitoring among pediatric patients and their parents. Secondary aims include identifying concerns surrounding general anesthesia (GA), concerns surrounding EEG monitoring, cost and willingness to pay, and sociodemographic and medical factors shaping these attitudes. We conducted an exploratory cross-sectional survey at a tertiary pediatric hospital in Singapore between July 2022 and September 2025. Respondents were parents of children aged 1-18 years and children aged 12-18 scheduled for elective procedures under general anesthesia. A 16-item anonymized questionnaire assessed perceptions of intra-operative EEG monitoring, concerns about anesthesia, and attitudes regarding the cost of EEG monitoring. Of 400 respondents (100 children, 300 parents), 83.5% rated intra-operative brain monitoring as "very" or "quite" important and 93% reported feeling more reassured by its use. Children were most concerned about intraoperative awareness and failure to awaken, whereas parents were most concerned about anesthetic side effects and dosage. Parents with higher education and whose children had prior anesthetic exposure reported greater reassurance from EEG monitoring. Cost was the leading concern regarding EEG monitoring, particularly among parents from families residing in public housing. Despite this, most parents (75%) and children (59%) expressed willingness to pay for EEG monitoring. Pediatric patients and parents viewed intra-operative EEG monitoring as important and reassuring, and expressed willingness to support its implementation despite cost concerns. These findings suggest that families are unlikely to be a major barrier to EEG adoption and highlight the need for clinician- and system-level strategies to integrate EEG monitoring into family-centered pediatric anesthesia care.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence Enabled Dielectric Fingerprinting of Arrhythmogenic Substrates: A Precision Paradigm for Tissue Characterization Guided Cardiac Electrophysiology.
papers.abstract: Electrical and dielectric properties of the myocardium depend on its composition, fibrosis, edema, ischemia, and heat damage, and hence may play an important role in defining the electrophysiologic substrate. Local impedance and other impedance-based methods give information about these parameters that is available to clinicians, but not direct or substitutable for intrinsic conductivity and permittivity of the tissue. The use of artificial intelligence has been thoroughly studied for the ECGs, electrograms, images, and computational data analysis, but not for dielectric or impedance measurements. The study aims to review the scientific basis of dielectric properties of heart muscle critically in cardiology and electrophysiology, to differentiate between existing clinical and conceptual applications of myocardial dielectrics, and to estimate current and potential contributions of artificial intelligence to their interpretation. The current work represents a structured narrative review in PubMed, Scopus, and Google Scholar databases from inception until May 2026 based on various combinations of keywords that refer to myocardial impedance, dielectric properties, conductivity, permittivity, local impedance, dielectric imaging, cardiac electrophysiology, catheter ablation, machine learning, and artificial intelligence. This review included experimental, ex vivo, animal, computational, and human studies related to myocardial dielectric properties and their use in electrophysiology. Evidence was classified according to four categories: direct human clinical evidence; preclinical/translation evidence; indirect evidence from related techniques; and extrapolation concept. As a result of heterogeneity between studies, sensing technologies, and outcomes, the results have been analyzed narratively. Evidence regarding the usage of AI algorithms, which have been primarily trained on myocardial dielectric or catheter-based local impedance data, is extremely scarce and mostly consists of preclinical or ex vivo data. On the contrary, the majority of clinically used AI algorithms in the field of electrophysiology make use of ECG data, intracardiac electrogram data, image processing, or computational modeling without any inputs related to dielectrics or local impedance. Dielectric sensing is an attractive supplement to traditional methods of voltage mapping and imaging, although the clinical readiness of dielectric sensing greatly varies depending on the application. At the present time, the existing data provide a basis for utilizing the local impedance measurement in the ablation procedure and evaluation of the myocardium properties, while the combination of artificial intelligence and dielectric sensing is still experimental. Before being introduced into the clinical electrophysiology practice, signal acquisition standardization and prospective multicenter trials are needed.
